article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: WhatsApp's built-in migration tool moves chats device-to-device over a local Wi-Fi connection using a QR code, without needing a Google Drive backup; on the new phone choose "Transfer your data using an Android device" and scan the QR code.
source: Google Android Help - Transfer WhatsApp data to a new Android
required_correction: Accurate description of the official Android-to-Android local QR chat-transfer flow; no correction needed.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: "Do not rely on Apple's older 'Move to iOS' app alone for chat history, since WhatsApp's own in-app migration flow (Settings > Chats > Chat Transfer on the sending device) is what carries chat content across platforms now" for both Android-to-iPhone and iPhone-to-Android moves.
source: WhatsApp Help Center - How to move chats from an Android device to an iPhone / How to move chats from an iPhone to an Android device
required_correction: This is backwards for the Android-to-iPhone direction, which is the flagged menu-path claim. The current official method for Android to iPhone still requires installing and running Apple's 'Move to iOS' app on the Android device as the entry point (it is not just an outdated fallback) - WhatsApp's own guidance leans on Move to iOS, then WhatsApp import happens after setup. Only the iPhone-to-Android direction has a true in-app WhatsApp flow: on iPhone, Settings > Chats > Transfer Chat History > Transfer to Android, paired with Settings > Chats > Move Chats to Android on the receiving Android device. The article should separate the two directions instead of implying one 'Chat Transfer' menu path replaces Move to iOS in both.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: On iPhone, back up to iCloud from Settings > Chats > Chat Backup before switching, then restore during WhatsApp setup on the new device using the same Apple ID and the same phone number.
source: Aggregated WhatsApp official-flow reporting (Wondershare, iMore, Techbout); primary faq.whatsapp.com pages returned truncated content and could not be fetched directly
required_correction: Menu path and same-Apple-ID/same-number requirement are consistently corroborated across secondary sources and match longstanding WhatsApp iOS behavior, but the primary WhatsApp FAQ page content could not be directly retrieved to confirm current exact wording - verify against a live WhatsApp iOS build before publishing given the article's own flag about menu-path currency.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: Every transfer method requires using the same phone number to verify WhatsApp on the new device as was registered on the old one.
source: WhatsApp Help Center / Google Android Help - Transfer WhatsApp data to a new Android
required_correction: Accurate; WhatsApp verification is tied to the phone number across all transfer methods.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: Starred messages carry over on same-platform transfers, but star status doesn't always survive a cross-platform move (Android to iPhone or the reverse).
required_correction: No official WhatsApp documentation found specifically addressing star-status persistence during cross-platform transfers. Either cite a source or soften to 'may not survive' framing pending verification.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: WhatsApp Business catalog items, saved quick replies, and labels are tied to the business profile data and transfer along with the chat backup.
required_correction: No official WhatsApp source found confirming catalog/labels/quick-replies reliably survive a device transfer. Add a citation or reframe as advice to double-check rather than an established fact.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: Transfers fail midway more often from insufficient free space on the new phone than from any other cause.
required_correction: Presented as a comparative statistic with no source. Either cite WhatsApp support data on failure causes or rewrite as general advice ('insufficient storage is a common cause of failed transfers') without the unsupported comparison.

article_title: How to Transfer WhatsApp Chats to a New Phone Without Losing History
claim: Keeping the old phone powered off but intact for a couple of weeks after a transfer is a cheap safety net.
required_correction: Reasonable practical advice, not a factual claim requiring a source.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: Xiaomi and Redmi call their app-cloning feature Dual Apps, Samsung calls it Dual Messenger, OnePlus and Oppo call it Parallel Apps or Clone Apps.
source: Aggregated manufacturer feature naming (MakeUseOf, mobilemasr) consistent with Samsung/Xiaomi/OnePlus own settings menus
required_correction: Naming is accurate and current: Xiaomi/Redmi = Dual Apps, Samsung = Dual Messenger, OnePlus = Parallel Apps, Oppo/Realme = Clone Apps.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: WhatsApp has added native support for linking a second account within the same app on devices with dual SIM, found under Settings > Accounts > Add Account inside the app.
source: Android Authority / GSMArena - WhatsApp multiple accounts support rollout reporting
required_correction: The native multiple-accounts feature itself is real and has rolled out to Android/iOS, requiring a second number via dual SIM, eSIM, or virtual number. The exact menu path 'Settings > Accounts > Add Account' could not be confirmed against a primary WhatsApp source (WhatsApp's own FAQ pages were inaccessible during verification) - check this wording against a current WhatsApp build before publishing, per the article's own flagged concern about menu-path currency.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: You need an active phone number to verify the second account, which usually means a second physical SIM or an eSIM - WhatsApp does not allow one number to run two accounts.
source: Android Authority - WhatsApp multi-account support reporting
required_correction: Accurate; each WhatsApp account, native or cloned, requires its own unique phone number for verification.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: A cloned WhatsApp instance maintains entirely separate backup settings from the original, so Google Drive or local backup needs to be configured independently - check Settings > Chats > Chat Backup inside the cloned app.
source: WhatsApp standard backup menu behavior (consistent across app instances since a clone runs the same app)
required_correction: Accurate; a cloned/sandboxed instance has its own independent backup configuration under the same standard WhatsApp menu location.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: Some phone manufacturers apply aggressive battery optimization to cloned or dual apps by default, which can delay or suppress notifications for the second account without any obvious error message.
required_correction: Widely reported user complaint in Android enthusiast communities (particularly for Xiaomi/Oppo/Vivo skins), but no single authoritative manufacturer document confirms this as a stated default behavior. Treat as corroborated community knowledge rather than a formally sourced fact, or add a specific manufacturer citation.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: Running two WhatsApp instances, whether cloned or natively linked, does use somewhat more background battery and RAM than a single account.
source: General Android OS resource-management behavior
required_correction: Uncontroversial technical fact; two active app instances/notification services consume more resources than one. No specific citation needed.

article_title: How to Set Up a Second WhatsApp Number on One Phone
claim: For someone handling a high volume of business messages, a fully separate device keeps work notifications from interrupting a personal one and avoids the performance overhead of two instances.
required_correction: Subjective recommendation, not a checkable factual claim.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: A built-in screen recorder has shipped on every Android phone since version 11, tucked into the Quick Settings panel.
source: Android community/enthusiast documentation of the Android 11 release (Gadget Hacks)
required_correction: Accurate - the native Screen Record Quick Settings tile was introduced with Android 11 (2020). Note some OEM skins/budget devices still ship without it enabled, which the article does separately acknowledge.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: Streaming apps like Netflix or Prime Video use content protection (Widevine DRM) that deliberately blocks screen recording, showing a black screen even though playback looks normal on the display.
source: Widevine DRM technical explainers (BuyDRM / Bitmovin community)
required_correction: Accurate. On Widevine L1 (hardware-secured) devices, protected video is decoded in a secure area never exposed to the recording pipeline, producing black frames; this is intentional content protection, not a recorder bug.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: Recording an actual phone call through the built-in screen recorder is blocked on many phones by design, and separately, call-recording legality varies by context in India depending on consent.
source: Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 (Section 5(2)); Information Technology Act, 2000 (Sections 66 & 72); legal explainers discussing Article 21 right to privacy
required_correction: This is the flagged claim - it needed a citation and it had none. The underlying premise is correct but should be stated more precisely: India has no dedicated 'call recording law.' Recording is generally treated as permissible under one-party consent (legal if you are a participant in the call); a third party intercepting or recording a call they are not part of risks liability under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 (unauthorized interception) and Sections 66/72 of the IT Act, 2000 (unauthorized access/disclosure of electronic information), and can implicate the Article 21 constitutional right to privacy. Add this citation and the one-party-consent clarification rather than leaving the claim as a vague, uncited generalization.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: For phones running Android 10 or earlier without a native recorder, connecting to a PC and using the ADB command adb shell screenrecord captures the screen without installing anything on the phone; it requires enabling Developer Options and USB debugging first.
source: Android Developers - Android Debug Bridge (adb) documentation
required_correction: Accurate. The screenrecord shell utility has been available via adb since Android 4.4 (well before Android 10), and does require Developer Options and USB debugging enabled.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: Xiaomi devices running MIUI or HyperOS sometimes list their screen recorder under Settings > Additional settings > Screen recorder instead of only the quick tile.
source: Xiaomi/community MIUI-HyperOS documentation (Wondershare, XimiTime)
required_correction: Menu path matches current MIUI/HyperOS structure; no correction needed.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: Every major video calling app displays its own on-screen notice or icon when a screen recording is active during a call, meaning this isn't a covert method and other participants will generally be able to see recording is happening.
source: Reporting on Zoom/Google Meet/WhatsApp screen-recording detection behavior (EaseUS, Kingshiper)
required_correction: This overstates the case and should be corrected. WhatsApp itself does not detect or notify call participants when someone is screen-recording a WhatsApp video call using an external tool like Android's native recorder - there is no on-screen indicator. Zoom and Google Meet only notify participants when their own built-in in-app recording feature is used, not when a participant uses an independent screen recorder, which is exactly the scenario this article covers. The claim should be corrected or removed to avoid giving readers false confidence that this method is always visible to others.

article_title: How to Screen Record on Android Without a Third-Party App
claim: Samsung's version, found through Quick Settings, includes extra options like S Pen annotation and front-camera overlay for reaction-style recordings.
source: Samsung One UI screen recorder feature documentation (aggregated)
required_correction: Consistent with well-documented Samsung One UI screen recorder features; no correction needed.

article_title: Digital Decluttering: How to Clean Up Years of Phone Photos and Files
claim: Most gallery apps also keep a recently-deleted folder for 30 to 60 days as a safety net.
source: Google Photos Help - Restore recently deleted photos & videos
required_correction: Matches Google Photos policy exactly: 60 days for backed-up items, 30 days for items that aren't backed up. Accurate as a general range for major gallery apps.

article_title: Digital Decluttering: How to Clean Up Years of Phone Photos and Files
claim: WhatsApp-forwarded images saved automatically to your gallery are usually where the bulk of storage goes.
source: WhatsApp default media auto-save behavior (widely documented app setting)
required_correction: Accurate; WhatsApp's default 'save to gallery' setting saves incoming media automatically unless the user disables it.

article_title: Digital Decluttering: How to Clean Up Years of Phone Photos and Files
claim: Most phones have a built-in tool or setting that flags similar photos automatically.
required_correction: True for some major galleries (Google Photos' duplicate/'free up space' suggestions on some Android builds, Samsung Gallery's similar-photo grouping) but not a universal built-in feature across 'most phones' as implied. Name specific apps or add a caveat rather than generalizing.

article_title: Digital Decluttering: How to Clean Up Years of Phone Photos and Files
claim: Several phones now offer an automatic rule to delete screenshots or downloaded files after a set number of days if they haven't been opened again.
required_correction: No authoritative source found confirming this as a widespread native OS capability. Age-based auto-delete for screenshots/downloads exists in some third-party file managers and a few OEM skins, but isn't a general Android/iOS feature as implied. Soften the claim or cite a specific manufacturer's documentation.

article_title: Digital Decluttering: How to Clean Up Years of Phone Photos and Files
claim: Going through years of photos one by one would eat an entire weekend; working in bulk filters first gets the same result in a couple of hours instead.
required_correction: Subjective time estimate used as a framing device, not a checkable fact.

article_title: Digital Decluttering: How to Clean Up Years of Phone Photos and Files
claim: Videos take up disproportionately more storage than photos and are reviewed far less often once saved.
source: General file-size/media-format knowledge
required_correction: Uncontroversial technical fact; video files are substantially larger per item than photos. No specific citation needed.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: The padlock icon only means the connection is encrypted; it says nothing about who owns the server. A scammer can get a free HTTPS certificate for a phishing page in minutes.
source: General web/browser security guidance on TLS certificates and free CA issuance (e.g. Let's Encrypt)
required_correction: Accurate and well-established: HTTPS/the padlock indicates transport encryption only, not site legitimacy, and free automated certificate authorities make HTTPS trivial for attackers to obtain.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: The part that matters is the registered domain: the last two segments right before the first single slash after the protocol.
required_correction: This heuristic breaks for the multi-part public suffixes common in exactly the India-relevant examples the article uses elsewhere (e.g. a bank at 'sbi.co.in' or a government site at '.gov.in') - 'the last two segments' would read as 'co.in' or 'gov.in', not the actual registrable domain. Add a caveat about ccTLD second-level domains (.co.in, .org.in, .net.in, .gov.in) or readers will misjudge precisely the domains most relevant to Indian phishing scams.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: India's CERT-In accepts phishing report submissions through its website.
source: CERT-In Directions under Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000 (28 April 2022), Annexure I
required_correction: Accurate; 'Identity Theft, spoofing and phishing attacks' is explicitly listed as a mandatorily reportable incident type, reportable via incident@cert-in.org.in, phone, or the CERT-In website.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: Chrome, Firefox, and Edge all include a built-in safe browsing or phishing protection feature that checks visited sites against a known-bad list, generally switched on by default.
source: Google Chrome Help - Choose your Safe Browsing protection level
required_correction: Accurate; Chrome ships with Standard Safe Browsing protection enabled by default, and Firefox/Edge use comparable phishing and malware blocklist protections enabled by default.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: Given how much everyday payment in India runs through UPI QR codes, QR code phishing ("quishing") is its own growing problem in India.
required_correction: The underlying mechanism (malicious QR codes redirecting UPI payment requests) is real and has been reported, but 'growing problem' is asserted without any statistic or source. Cite a specific advisory (e.g., an RBI, NPCI, or CERT-In notice on QR-code fraud) or soften the claim to avoid implying a measured trend.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: Having two-factor authentication enabled on email, banking, and other important accounts means a stolen password alone usually isn't enough for an attacker to get in.
source: General security best-practice guidance on multi-factor authentication
required_correction: Standard, well-established security guidance; no specific citation needed beyond general MFA principles.

article_title: How to Tell If a Link Is a Phishing Scam Before You Click It
claim: A more advanced typosquatting variant uses characters from other alphabets that render identically to Latin letters (homoglyph attacks), though this is rarer in everyday scams.
source: General security literature on IDN homograph/homoglyph phishing attacks
required_correction: Accurate description of a recognized phishing technique (IDN homograph attacks); no correction needed.

source: Google Account Help - Manage your Timeline data

claim: Visit myadcenter.google.com to see the categories Google has inferred about you and to switch off personalized ads entirely or remove specific categories.

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: India's CERT-In rules (in effect since 2022) require VPN providers offering service in India to maintain certain customer logs (name, validated address, usage period, IP addresses assigned) for a defined retention period.
source: CERT-In Directions under Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000 (No. 20(3)/2022-CERT-In, dated 28 April 2022), clause (v)
required_correction: Exact match to the directive's clause (v): validated names of subscribers, period of hire/dates, IPs allotted, validated address and contact numbers, retained for 5 years or longer as mandated by law. The article could add the specific 5-year figure for extra precision instead of only 'a defined retention period.'

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: Many major consumer VPN providers responded to the CERT-In rules by removing their physical servers from India rather than complying, meaning your "India" server location may not exist and traffic may be routed abroad.
source: TechRadar / Inc42 / TechCrunch reporting on ExpressVPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, and Proton VPN removing physical Indian servers in 2022
required_correction: Accurate. ExpressVPN, Surfshark, NordVPN, Proton VPN and others pulled physical servers from India around the CERT-In directive's June 2022 effective date and now offer 'India' locations via virtual servers hosted abroad.

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: A VPN does not stop malware, and it does not protect you from phishing - a fake bank login page is exactly as convincing over a VPN as without one.
source: ExpressVPN / NordVPN official explainers on VPN limitations
required_correction: Accurate; consistent with VPN providers' own official statements about the limits of encryption-only protection against malware and phishing.

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: A VPN app creates an encrypted connection to a VPN server and routes all traffic through it; websites you visit see the VPN server's IP address and location instead of yours.
source: General VPN technical mechanism (standard tunneling/encryption description)
required_correction: Correct, standard description of how VPN tunneling and IP masking works; no correction needed.

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: A "no-logs" claim is only as good as the company's honesty and jurisdiction, and isn't independently verifiable by an ordinary user - even audited ones rely on trusting the audit's scope.
required_correction: Reasonable, widely-shared security-community viewpoint, but an interpretive judgment rather than a directly checkable fact.

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: Running servers costs money, so a free VPN's business model is very often selling aggregated or even individual traffic data to advertisers.
required_correction: This is a widely repeated claim in security journalism (past academic studies of free Android VPN apps found many contained trackers or shared data), but as written it is an unsourced generalization ('very often'). Cite a concrete study (e.g., peer-reviewed research on free VPN app data practices) rather than asserting it as self-evident fact.

article_title: What a VPN Actually Protects You From, and What It Does Not
claim: Some VPN apps offer split tunneling, letting you choose which apps route through the VPN and which use your normal connection directly.
source: Standard VPN feature documentation (general)
required_correction: Accurately described, standard VPN feature; no correction needed.
